doing: darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing
counting the umbrellas on their hooks
pouring tea nobody asked for
writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink

looks.text: A broad woman in widow’s black and a gray cardigan, in a kitchen chair on the first landing, with a sock stretched over a darning egg.
A ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes.
Reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again.

ask: Sit down, then, and mind the basket. You want my evening, you’ll have it, and it’s the same as every evening, God help me.
My evening? I’ll give it to you the way Mr. Rafferty, God rest him, gave the news: all of it, slowly, with a pause for tea.
deflect: That’s one for the priest, not the landlady.
Now what would a widow on a landing know about that?
nobodyElse: And that’s the lot. If there’d been another one on my stairs, I’d have his name and his mother’s maiden name.
Nobody else. Nobody gets past the basket.

hours.7: Seven, I take my chair and the mending, and the house knows I’m on.
hours.8: Eight, I’ve the tea on and a sock on the egg and one ear on the door.
hours.9: Nine’s the quiet hour. You can hear a lodger think, if he does.
hours.10: Ten’s the rule. After ten I’m not a landlady, I’m a customs house.
hours.11: Eleven, I start listening for the late ones, the way you’d listen for rain.

refuse: I’ve kept a respectable house for thirty-one years, and I’ll not have it questioned on my own landing.
You can put that to the Sacred Heart in the hall. He’s heard worse from me.
ownUp: Ah, well. Mr. Rafferty always said I’d a face that couldn’t keep a thing past the second cup. Here it is.

ties.line: Miss Gutman pays on a Friday, early, in an envelope with her name on it, and I’d frame it if I didn’t need it.
Mr. Mabry comes in at four with his shoes in his hand so as not to wake me. I’m awake. It’s nice of him anyway.
Agnes is three weeks behind and cries when I mention it, so I’ve stopped mentioning it and started writing it down.
Mrs. Szabo carried a wardrobe up four flights on her own the day she came. I’ve never had a lodger I’d sooner have on the stairs, or argue with less.

secrets.text: She lets the attic to a man with his name on no paper anywhere, for cash, and tells the lodgers he’s her nephew from Cork.
She steams open the lodgers’ letters over the kettle on wet evenings, when she says the damp gets into the glue anyway.

asVictim.why: She knows everything that’s gone up her stairs in thirty-one years, and some of it would rather she didn’t.
asVictim.foundWith: her ring of keys in her lap and a darning egg still in one hand.

doing: sitting on the areaway steps with his pipe
shoveling coal into the boiler
answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench
sweeping a stoop he swept an hour ago

looks.text: A square man in a cardigan and a cloth cap on the areaway steps, so still with his pipe that you notice the smoke before the man.
Coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out.
A ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them.

ask: Same as every night. It’s a short story. You can stand for it.
Where was I. On the steps. You want it by the hour, I give it by the hour.
deflect: I fix radiators. I don’t fix that.
That’s upstairs business. I’m a cellar man.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. A rat. A rat doesn’t count.
That’s all. Nobody gets up that stoop without stepping on my shadow.

hours.7: Seven, I bank the boiler for the night. She sulks. Then she settles.
hours.8: Eight, I sit. Pipe. Steps. Street.
hours.9: Nine, the fourth floor bangs on the pipe. I bang back. That’s our conversation.
hours.10: Ten, I sweep the stoop. It doesn’t need it. I need it.
hours.11: Eleven, I look at the fire one more time, and then I look at the street one more time.

refuse: No. I said what I said. I’m a janitor, not a radio.
I don’t answer that one. You can stand there till spring.
ownUp: So. I tell you once, and then we don’t talk about it.

ties.line: Mrs. Krantz pays me twelve dollars a week and the coal. Most weeks, the coal.
Mrs. Sobel says I give her half a scuttle. I give her what the boiler gives. She can take it up with the boiler.
Meyer and me play checkers on the stoop Sundays. He cheats. I let him. Who else is he going to beat?

secrets.text: He sells the building’s coal by the sack to the undertaker over the Peacock, out the cellar door on Saturday nights, which is why the fourth floor is cold.

asVictim.why: He has a key to every flat in the building and a long memory for who goes into which.
asVictim.foundWith: his pipe gone cold in one pocket and a stub of chalk from the coal tally in the other.

doing: counting glasses onto a towel
wiping flour off the gin bottles
looking in on the ovens through the door marked FLOUR
slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats

looks.text: A barrel of a man in a baker’s white shirt with the sleeves rolled, flour to the elbows and gin to the wrists.
Eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years.
A row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911.

ask: Pull up a stool. I’ve been up since four, so if I fall asleep in the middle, wake me at the next hour.
My evening? Same as my morning, with gin where the flour goes. All right. From seven.
deflect: I bake bread and I pour drinks. Everything else, I let rise on its own.
Not a question for a barman. That’s for a barman’s lawyer, and I can’t afford one.
nobodyElse: That’s everybody. I counted the glasses twice.
Nobody else. If there was, there’s a glass I can’t account for, and there isn’t.

hours.7: Seven, I take the last tray out and unlock the door that says flour. One job stops, the other one starts.
hours.8: Eight’s the regulars. I pour before they ask. It saves them the strain.
hours.9: Nine, I count the glasses the first time. Count at nine, you know where you stand at two.
hours.10: Ten, I set the sponge for tomorrow’s rye between customers. Nobody’s ever complained the gin smelled of yeast.
hours.11: Eleven, the place goes quiet, and in a quiet bar you hear everything, whether you want it or not.

refuse: No. You want that, come back at four in the morning and ask the dough.
I said what I said, with flour on my hands, which is how you know it’s honest.
ownUp: You caught me with my hands in the bowl. Here’s how it was.

ties.line: Sid lent me for the new oven, and now he sits in my back booth for nothing and calls it interest.
Assunta and I walked out in nineteen-nine. She said my bread was heavy. A hard thing to hear from a woman who cooks with that much lard.

secrets.text: He keeps Assunta Greco’s letters from nineteen-nine in a tin at the bottom of the flour bin, under the flour.

asVictim.why: He owes Fishel for the oven, and he knows which of his customers owe Fishel more.
asVictim.foundWith: flour to the elbows and a glass towel over his shoulder.

doing: looking through the slot in the steel door
knitting a muffler with no end in sight
eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool
explaining to a large man why he is going home

looks.text: A big woman on a stool behind the steel door, in a beaded dress and a man’s overcoat, with forearms like a stevedore’s.
A nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it.
Big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss.

ask: My night. Fine. It was short and I was standing up for it.
Where was I. On that door. Where else does a door go?
deflect: I’ve thrown bigger questions than that down a flight of stairs.
Ask me something with a weight class.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. I’d remember. I don’t like enough faces to forget any.
That’s the lot. Anybody else came to my slot, he’s still out on the sidewalk.

hours.7: Seven, the slot opens and I eat my supper off a plate on my knee. Nobody worth turning away comes at seven.
hours.8: Eight, the dinner crowd. Dinner crowd’s easy. They only want to sit down.
hours.9: Nine, the music starts and the faces get worse.
hours.10: Ten’s when the uptown people come down slumming. I make them wait. It’s good for them.
hours.11: Eleven, I eat my pickle. Everybody who knows me knows not to knock during the pickle.

refuse: No. And I’ve said no to men twice your size, on worse stairs.
You’re knocking on the wrong door.
ownUp: Two falls out of three. You got the first. Here’s the rest.

ties.line: Mrs. Rafferty is the only landlady on the East Side who didn’t ask me what I used to do. She asked if I could carry a wardrobe.
Lola’s all right. She sells cigarettes to people I let in, and buys things off people I shouldn’t have.
Doyle had my brother sent up for a year over a crap game. He still tips his hat to me in the street. One day I’ll take the hat.

secrets.text: On Mondays, when the Peacock is dark, she wrestles one bout in a hood at the card room over the garage, as the Masked Countess, for twenty dollars.

asVictim.why: She has turned away half the East Side at that slot, and some of them took it personally.
asVictim.foundWith: her knitting in her lap and the key to the steel door on a string round her wrist.

doing: marking crosses on his seating chart
mouthing the third act from the back of the house
sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery
pointing his flashlight at a man who is talking

looks.text: A small old man in a maroon uniform with brass buttons, two of them from a different uniform.
A white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves.
His seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper.

ask: The whole evening? Like the play, then: three acts, no intermission, and you’ll forgive me if I do the voices.
Sit. Not there, that’s a good seat. Here. Now, from the overture.
deflect: That, my friend, is not in the script.
Forty years in the theater teaches a man one thing: when you don’t know your line, look at the floor.
nobodyElse: And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.
That’s the house. A small house, but an honest one.

hours.7: Seven, I open the doors and take up the chart. Every seat sold, a cross. I’m very good at crosses.
hours.8: Eight, the curtain goes up, and I go to the back of the house, where an usher belongs and an actor once didn’t.
hours.9: Nine, the second act. I could do it in my sleep, and some nights I think I have.
hours.10: Ten, I go round with the flashlight and wake the ones who only came in for the warm.
hours.11: Eleven, they go home, and I go round picking up gloves. Nobody ever comes back for a glove.

refuse: Some lines an actor improves by cutting. I’m cutting that one.
No. An usher shows people to their seats. He doesn’t show them his.
ownUp: The curtain comes down, the actor takes off the beard. Here is the truth.

ties.line: Stanislaw plays checkers the way he stokes a boiler: slowly, and he thinks he’s winning.
Lazar Belkin took the rabbi from me in nineteen-twelve. I’ve shown people to their seats to watch him do it ever since.
Tillie married my sister’s boy, and then she unmarried him. I kept her. He was never much of a nephew.

secrets.text: He has written a play in four acts, and after the house empties he reads it aloud from the stage to the empty seats, doing all the parts.

asVictim.why: He has watched the Lyric from the back of the house for forty years, and he could tell you who sat with whom.
asVictim.foundWith: his seating chart under one arm and his flashlight still on, pointing at the floor.

doing: writing covers in the book at his stand
folding napkins into shapes nobody asked for
seating a man who would rather have stood
holding a fork up to the light

looks.text: A tall man in a tailcoat gone green at the seams, standing at a book on a stand by the door like a bishop at a lectern.
Hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets.
A white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it.

ask: Certainly, sir. Allow me to show you to my evening. This way.
My evening, sir, was conducted with the dignity of the house. I’ll take you through the courses.
deflect: I couldn’t say, sir. A head waiter sees everything and remembers only the gratuity.
That would be a matter for the management, sir, and the management is in Florida.
nobodyElse: And that, sir, is every cover. I don’t lose covers.
No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so.

hours.7: Seven, sir: the early covers. People who dine at seven are not interesting, but they tip.
hours.8: Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat.
hours.9: Nine, the theater crowd, who want everything at once and the bill before it.
hours.10: Ten, the room thins and I count the napkins. One learns a great deal from napkins.
hours.11: Eleven, the late ones. I seat them near the kitchen. They never notice, and I never mention it.

refuse: I regret, sir, that particular dish is not available this evening.
No, sir. That table is reserved.
ownUp: Very well, sir. I’ll bring you the bill, itemized.

ties.line: Mrs. Greco runs that kitchen like a fortress and treats the dining room like the enemy. I am the dining room.
I owe Carmine Russo for a straight that turned out to be crooked. I pay him on Tuesdays out of my gratuities, and he counts it in front of me.

secrets.text: He pawns his good tailcoat at Wexler’s on Mondays and redeems it on Fridays, and sends the difference to a wife in Baltimore nobody on Grand Street has heard of.

asVictim.why: He owes Russo for a crooked straight, and he has written down the name and the hour of everybody who ever ate at Steinmetz’s.
asVictim.foundWith: the book of covers under his arm and a napkin in his breast pocket, folded into a swan.

doing: adding up the day’s fees in the cash book
writing appointment cards in her best hand
telling a man with a toothache to sit down and be brave
polishing the bell

looks.text: A small, bright girl in a white smock behind a desk with a brass bell on it, her pencil already raised before you’ve spoken.
A bob she cut herself with the surgery scissors, a little shorter on the left.
Teeth so perfect people assume the doctor did them; she was born with them, and she’ll tell you.

ask: Oh, I can do better than that. I can do it by the clock, the way I do the book.
Sit down, it won’t hurt. That’s what I tell all of them. Now: seven.
deflect: I’d have to look in the book, and the book’s locked, and the doctor has the key.
That’s between you and your dentist.
nobodyElse: And nobody else. Everybody rings the bell, even the ones who hate the bell.
That’s the lot. I’d know. I know people by their teeth.

hours.7: Seven’s the last appointments, the ones who couldn’t get off work, with their toothaches and their lunch pails.
hours.8: Eight, I do the day’s book, and the waiting room watches me do it.
hours.9: Nine, I lock the cash box and put the cover on the typewriter, and that’s my day.
hours.10: Ten, I put my feet in hot water and read somebody else’s movie magazine.
hours.11: Eleven, I’m asleep, or I’m lying there doing tomorrow’s book in my head.

refuse: No, I won’t say. The doctor says I have a mouth on me, and this is me closing it.
I’ve said all I’m saying. You can make another appointment.
ownUp: Oh, fine. I’ll tell you, but you have to let me tell it right, from the beginning.

ties.line: Mrs. Rafferty treats me like a daughter, which is lovely, and means I can’t come in after ten without a reason she likes.
Dr. Hirsch is the best dentist on Clinton Street, and she knows it, and she tells me so on Fridays instead of a raise.
Oscar Lieb took me dancing twice and talked about his uncle’s shop the whole time. I know the price of every ring in that window.

secrets.text: She keeps a second little book of what the patients say under the gas, and some of it is worth more than the fillings.

asVictim.why: She keeps a little book of what people say under the gas, and one of them has read it.
asVictim.foundWith: the appointment book in her handbag and a pencil behind her ear, sharpened at both ends.

doing: weighing a ring on the jeweler’s scales
writing a ticket in a slow, square hand
looking at a coat’s lining before its outside
counting the day’s takings into a cigar box, twice

looks.text: A thin old man behind brass bars in a black skullcap and sleeve garters, with a jeweler’s loupe in one eye that he forgets to take out when he looks at people.
A gold watch chain across his vest, with a different watch on the end of it every time you see him.
Fingertips stained gray from tickets and newsprint and other people’s silver.

ask: My evening. Let me look at it first, the way I look at anything a man hands me. Hm. All right. It’s worth telling.
Sit. I give you the evening, you give me nothing, and I write you no ticket. A bargain.
deflect: That, I wouldn’t lend two dollars on.
A pawnbroker doesn’t ask where a thing came from. He asks how much. You’re asking the wrong question of the wrong man.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. Everybody who comes to the cage gets a ticket or a no, and I’ve given you the tickets and the no’s.
That’s all. I remember faces the way other men remember debts.

hours.7: Seven, the working men come with their Sunday suits, to get the money for Monday.
hours.8: Eight, the women come with the rings, and I am very kind, and I give them two dollars.
hours.9: Nine, I write up the day. Every ticket a line, and every line a story I don’t ask about.
hours.10: Ten, I lock the cage, and I sit in it anyway. Where else would I sit? It’s my chair.
hours.11: Eleven, I count the back room. You’d be surprised how often a coat goes missing from a room full of coats nobody wants.

refuse: No. Some things I take in pledge, and some things I don’t take at any price.
That, I keep in the back room, with the coats.
ownUp: So. A man can only keep a thing so long before the interest is worth more than the thing.

ties.line: Oscar is my wife’s sister’s boy. I gave him a job so she would stop asking. Now she asks why I don’t pay him.
Belkin pledges his mother’s ring on Mondays and redeems it on Fridays. Last Friday, he didn’t. Forty dollars, and a ring I can’t sell, because everybody knows whose it is.
Sid Fishel buys from the same people I do, without a ticket and without a license, and he calls it competition.

secrets.text: He keeps a drawer of things he took in without tickets from men who never came back, and he wears their watches on his chain one at a time, a week each.

asVictim.why: Half the East Side has something in his window, and the other half wants it back without paying.
asVictim.foundWith: his loupe still in one eye and a blank pledge ticket in his fist.

doing: writing odds on the back of a menu
not drinking a cup of coffee
weighing a wristwatch in his palm without looking at it
reading the racing results with his lips moving

looks.text: A heavy man in a good gray suit gone shiny at the knees, in the back booth behind the flour sacks, with a pencil and a cup of cold coffee.
A diamond pinky ring a size too small, so that the finger has grown around it.
A pearl-gray fedora he never takes off indoors, because, he says, it’s worth more than the indoors.

ask: You want my night. I’ll give you odds it’s duller than you think. Even money. Sit.
Short version. I sat. People came to me. That’s the business.
deflect: I don’t take bets on that.
I’d need to see a form sheet before I said anything about anybody.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. Book’s closed.
That’s the field. No other runners.

hours.7: Seven, the book opens. First race of the night, you might say.
hours.8: Eight, the working men come for a dollar on tomorrow. I give them a pencil and some hope.
hours.9: Nine, I order a coffee. I don’t drink it. It’s company.
hours.10: Ten, the big money comes, if it comes. It comes in small bills, and nervous.
hours.11: Eleven, I add it up. Then I add it up again, because the first time it always comes out in my favor.

refuse: No bet.
You’re asking me to make a price on that. I don’t make a price on that.
ownUp: You’ve seen my card. I’ll show you the rest of the hand.

ties.line: Abe owes me four hundred for the oven. I take it out in booth.
Wexler gives a man a ticket and two dollars. I give him five and no questions. Who’s the crook?
Carmine runs a table that leans, and he took two of my best customers to lean on it.
Agnes owes me eleven on a horse called Mother’s Pride. I don’t chase girls for eleven dollars. I let them chase themselves.

secrets.text: He pays the alderman’s clerk to keep the police off Sokol’s, and charges Sokol for the same favor twice.

asVictim.why: He’s holding everybody’s money on tomorrow’s races, and a dead bookmaker pays nobody.
asVictim.foundWith: his gray fedora still on and a racing sheet folded to the third race.

doing: working the tables with her tray
looking at every wrist she passes
making change faster than a bank
fixing her lipstick in the back of a cigarette case

looks.text: A woman with a tray of cigarettes on a strap round her neck, in a short spangled dress and a smile she puts on with the lipstick.
A row of bangles up one arm that clink when she makes change, and two wristwatches on the other, neither of them hers.
A fur stole that is mostly rabbit and partly confidence.

ask: Cigars, cigarettes, alibis. What’ll it be, honey? Oh, the evening. Sure.
My night? Honey, I walked it in heels. Every step’s still in my feet.
deflect: I sell cigarettes. Questions are next door.
You want that, you’ll have to buy a pack first. Two packs.
nobodyElse: That’s everybody, honey. I’d have sold them something.
Nobody. Me and the tray, and the tray doesn’t talk.

hours.7: Seven, I’m fixing my face. Takes an hour. Takes longer every year.
hours.8: Eight, I fill the tray. Luckies on top, the rest underneath.
hours.9: Nine, I start on the room. You smile at the men and you look at the wrists.
hours.10: Ten, my feet start talking. I don’t listen. I can’t afford to.
hours.11: Eleven, I count the tray. What’s gone tells me what kind of night it’s been.

refuse: Sorry, honey. That one’s not on the tray.
No sale.
ownUp: Fine, honey. You got me, and you didn’t even have to buy a pack.

ties.line: Ruby looks out for me. Ruby looks out for everybody, through a slot, with a face like a shut door.
Earl writes me a song every time we break up. He’s got a whole act now.
I’m two months behind with Mrs. Krantz, and she sends the janitor up to look sad at my door.
Oscar owes me twenty for a cigarette case that turned out to be his uncle’s. I gave the case back. He didn’t give the twenty.

secrets.text: She’s still married, as far as she knows, to a man in Hoboken, and when he turns up at the Peacock she pays him to go away again.

asVictim.why: She has bought things off half the thieves on Chrystie Street, and she remembers which half.
asVictim.foundWith: her cigarette tray still on its strap and a wristwatch tucked in her stocking top.

doing: sharpening instruments on a little stone
reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead
explaining to a grown man that it will only pinch
smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window

looks.text: A tall woman in a white coat with the sleeves turned back twice, precisely, and a dental mirror in her breast pocket like a fountain pen.
Steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you.
Very clean hands with very short nails, and a gold wedding band she wears on a chain round her neck instead of on the hand.

ask: Of course. Open wide. I mean the notebook. From seven, then, and stop me if anything hurts.
I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun.
deflect: That isn’t a dental question, and I don’t give opinions outside the mouth.
You’re probing, and I don’t see why I should sit still for it.
nobodyElse: No one else. I’d have noticed. I notice teeth.
That’s all. I don’t care for company in the evening. They want to show me their molars.

hours.7: At seven I’m usually thinking about supper and not getting it.
hours.8: Eight, I start to want a cigarette, and I make myself wait till nine. Discipline.
hours.9: Nine, I have the cigarette. One. I make it last like a good filling.
hours.10: Ten, I like an argument. They’re harder to come by than cigarettes.
hours.11: Eleven, I’m reading something I won’t admit to. Medical journals, I tell people.

refuse: No. I don’t answer that, and I don’t need gas to keep from it.
This consultation is over.
ownUp: I suppose it’s better out than in. That’s what I tell everybody.

ties.line: Pearl keeps the book like a jailer and the waiting room like a church. I’d pay her more if I had it, and some weeks I tell her so.
Carmine Russo has my marker for three hundred dollars, and he pats his breast pocket whenever he sees me.
Bea Lowenthal and I have had Sunday lunch for ten years. She has never once asked me to look at her teeth.

secrets.text: She plays poker at the card room over the garage, which she swore off at Easter in front of witnesses.
She sells the gold from old fillings to Wexler by the pennyweight, and doesn’t mention it to the patients it came out of.

asVictim.why: She owes Russo three hundred dollars and has stopped paying him, on principle.
asVictim.foundWith: her spectacles folded in her breast pocket beside the dental mirror.

doing: writing pledge tickets for his uncle
trying on a coat from the back room
polishing a trombone nobody will redeem
telling a customer what his own watch is worth

looks.text: A thin young man in sleeve garters behind the counter, in a waistcoat cut for somebody broader.
Clothes better than his wages and each a different size, as if he’d been dressed by several generous uncles.
A silk scarf with somebody else’s monogram on it, worn with the monogram tucked in.

ask: Sure, I’ll tell you. I tell everybody everything. That’s my trouble, my uncle says.
My night? Nothing much. Ask me about anybody’s watch, though. Now that’s interesting.
deflect: Couldn’t tell you. My uncle tells me what to know, and he didn’t tell me that.
Look, I just write the tickets.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. Just me and about four hundred coats.
That’s everybody. I’d have noticed. I notice clothes.

hours.7: Seven, I’m always starving. A fellow stuck behind a counter all day gets an appetite for everything.
hours.8: Eight, I start thinking about what to wear. I’ve got a lot to choose from. Don’t ask.
hours.9: Nine’s too early for anything good and too late for anything respectable.
hours.10: Ten’s when a fellow’s clothes start doing the talking, if he picked the right ones.
hours.11: Eleven’s my hour. A fellow’s got to have one.

refuse: Nope. That one I’m keeping, ticket and all.
Ask my uncle. He’s the one with the license.
ownUp: Look, don’t tell my uncle. Here’s the honest version. It’s shorter.

ties.line: Pearl’s sore because I talked about the shop. What else have I got to talk about? I’m in it twelve hours a day.
Uncle Ignatz pays me eleven dollars a week and calls it an education.
Vinnie drives me home at half fare because I tell him who’s pawned what. He says it’s for his education too.
I owe Lola twenty dollars over a cigarette case. It was a misunderstanding, and she understands it perfectly.

secrets.text: He wears the unredeemed pledges out at night, a dead man’s tuxedo when he can get it, and goes dancing at the Peacock in it.

asVictim.why: He talks about everybody’s pledges to anybody who’ll listen, and some of those pledges were never meant to be talked about.
asVictim.foundWith: a tuxedo two sizes too big, with a pledge ticket still pinned inside the lapel.

doing: dealing himself a hand of solitaire
counting a stack of bills by the edge
adding an ashtray to the table
sitting with his back to the wall

looks.text: A neat dark man in shirtsleeves and a green eyeshade, at the head of the table with his back to the wall.
Soft white hands that are always shuffling a deck, even in church, his mother-in-law says.
A pinstripe suit pressed to a knife edge, and one gold tooth that shows when he wins.

ask: Sure. Cut the deck. I’ll deal you the evening.
My night’s a short hand. I’ll show it face up.
deflect: I don’t play that game.
That’s a side bet. I don’t take side bets.
nobodyElse: Nobody else at the table.
That’s the hand. No more cards.

hours.7: Seven, I eat. A man shouldn’t deal hungry. He gets generous.
hours.8: Eight, I like to be sitting down with my back to a wall. Any wall.
hours.9: Nine, I watch. I always watch at nine. It’s when people get brave.
hours.10: Ten, everybody I know starts needing a loan. I give it. I remember it.
hours.11: Eleven, I count. Money, mostly. Sometimes sheep.

refuse: Fold.
I’m out. Deal around me.
ownUp: You called. I’ll show.

ties.line: Gus is good for it. Gus is slow for it, but he’s good.
The doctor plays poker the way she pulls teeth: no hesitation, no mercy, and no idea when to stop.
Sid thinks every dollar on the East Side is a dollar he lost. Some of them, he did. To me.
My mother-in-law crosses herself when I come to Sunday dinner, and then she gives me the biggest plate. That’s family.

secrets.text: The decks at the card room are shaved, and he shaves them himself, in the closet where the spare decks are kept.

asVictim.why: He holds markers on half the neighborhood, and a marker dies with the man who holds it.
asVictim.foundWith: a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand.

doing: practicing a death scene in a shop window
signing a program nobody asked him to sign
eating herring in a dressing gown
telling a story about Odessa in 1899

looks.text: A large, handsome ruin of a man in a velvet-collared coat, with a silver-topped cane he doesn’t need and uses for pointing.
Hair dyed a black that nature never tried, and greasepaint still in the creases by his ears.
A ring on every finger but one, and a pale band of skin on that one.

ask: My evening! Ah. Sit. As I give everything to my public: from the beginning, with feeling.
Where was Belkin tonight? Everywhere a man of the theater should be, my friend. In order, then.
deflect: Belkin does not dignify that. Belkin has played kings.
I’m an artist. Ask me about art.
nobodyElse: Alone. A great actor is always alone, even in a crowd. Especially in a crowd.
No one else. Only Belkin, and Belkin’s thoughts.

hours.7: Seven is when a man of the theater begins to feel his public waiting for him, wherever he is.
hours.8: Eight o’clock, my friend, is a curtain, whether or not there is a curtain.
hours.9: Nine, I grow thoughtful. Ask anyone. It’s very becoming.
hours.10: Ten, I am at my best. I have been told so by critics, two of them sober.
hours.11: Eleven, I begin to feel my age, and I refuse it, as I refuse all bad notices.

refuse: Belkin has nothing further to say. Belkin exits.
No. I have played Lear in Yiddish. I can play a man who doesn’t answer.
ownUp: The last act. Hold the curtain. Here is the truth, and I’ll try not to overplay it.

ties.line: Pinsky believes he’d have been a great rabbi. He is a great usher, and I tell him so, and somehow it doesn’t help.
Wexler has my mother’s ring in his window, where the whole Bowery can see it. He puts it there for that.
Tillie Moskin is the best ingénue on Second Avenue, and she wants my part. My part is a rabbi of sixty. She is twenty-four. That’s ambition.
I borrowed from Mrs. Krantz to get the ring back from Wexler, and then the money was needed elsewhere. That’s the theater.

secrets.text: When he’s short, he pledges the Lyric’s own silver candlesticks at Wexler’s and has them back on the stage before anybody counts them.

asVictim.why: He owes Wexler, owes Mrs. Krantz, and stands between Tillie Moskin and the part she wants.
asVictim.foundWith: his greasepaint still on and a program in his coat pocket, signed to himself.

doing: running her lines into a hand mirror
eating a knish in full costume
reading Variety for parts uptown
taking off greasepaint with cold cream

looks.text: A slim young woman in a peasant girl’s shawl and red skirt, with stage rouge on cheeks that don’t need it.
Big dark eyes that she knows how to use, and uses.
A copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news.

ask: Oh, my evening. Let me do it properly. You have to set the scene, or it doesn’t play.
Sure, ask me anything. I’m rehearsing for being famous, so I might as well practice my interviews.
deflect: That isn’t my line. I don’t do lines that aren’t mine.
Ask me again when I’m on Broadway. I’ll have a man who answers that.
nobodyElse: Just me. A girl alone in the big city. You could put it on a poster.
Nobody else. Not even an audience, and believe me, I looked.

hours.7: Seven’s my nervous hour. Every actress has one, and mine’s at seven.
hours.8: Eight, I’m always hungry, and I never eat. You can’t, at eight. You might need to look tragic later.
hours.9: Nine, I start feeling like somebody. It wears off by midnight, like the rouge.
hours.10: Ten’s when I think about uptown. Everybody on Second Avenue thinks about uptown at ten.
hours.11: Eleven, I’m tired, and I won’t admit it, because tired is for the chorus.

refuse: No. I’m not playing that scene.
I don’t do that part. Get somebody else to read it.
ownUp: Curtain up. Here’s what really happened, and I don’t come out of it as well as the heroine.

ties.line: Uncle Meyer still calls me his niece. I divorced his nephew, not him.
Mr. Belkin pays me nineteen a week and lets me die in his arms in the third act. He thinks the nineteen is the generous part.
Vinnie and me went steady all last summer. Then I got a part. He still won’t take my fare, which is either love or bad business.

secrets.text: She meets a producer from uptown in the curtained booth at Steinmetz’s, where nobody from Second Avenue would be seen eating, and she hasn’t told Belkin she’s been offered a part.

asVictim.why: She’s leaving the Lyric for uptown and taking the company’s best notices with her.
asVictim.foundWith: an uptown contract in her handbag, unsigned, and a stick of greasepaint.

doing: writing a tune on the back of a menu
oiling the valves of his cornet
tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers
eating pie at four in the morning

looks.text: A lean man in a tuxedo with the tie undone, and a cornet under one arm that he holds as if somebody might ask for it back.
A pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been.
A callus on his upper lip from the mouthpiece, which he touches when he’s thinking.

ask: Sure. Let me count it off for you. One, two, a-one two three four: seven o’clock.
My night? I’ll play it straight, no improvising. Takes the fun out, but you asked.
deflect: I don’t read that kind of music.
That’s not in my key.
nobodyElse: Nobody else. Solo.
Just me. No band, no singer, no applause.

hours.7: Seven, I warm up my lip. Wherever I am, the lip comes too.
hours.8: Eight’s a slow hour. Slow tempo. I like a slow eight.
hours.9: Nine’s when the night picks up the beat, whether you’re ready or not.
hours.10: Ten, I start hearing tunes in everything: car horns, the el, a woman laughing two streets off.
hours.11: Eleven’s the hour for the last good tune. After that everybody’s playing for tips.

refuse: No. That’s a number I don’t play.
I’ll sit this one out.
ownUp: Take it from the top, and I’ll play it the way it was written.

ties.line: Mrs. Rafferty feeds me pie at four in the morning and lectures me with her mouth full. Best room I ever had.
Lola and me were a number for two years. She still sings the bridge wrong to annoy me.
Miss Lowenthal tells every kid on Orchard Street that jazz will ruin their wrists. Half of them are in my audience by sixteen.
Sol Teitel keeps the loudest ties on Orchard Street under a cloth for me. He’s the only man below Fourteenth Street who understands a bandleader.

secrets.text: He sells his tunes for cash, no name on them, to a man from Tin Pan Alley who meets him at a table by the oven wall at Sokol’s, and then hears them on the radio under somebody else’s name.

asVictim.why: He knows which uptown bandleader’s hits are really his, and he’s started saying so.
asVictim.foundWith: his cornet in its case and a page of music in his inside pocket with no title on it.

doing: scrubbing a pot as if it had insulted her
tasting the gravy off a wooden spoon
crossing herself when the fat spits
carrying a covered pot out the alley door

looks.text: A short, wide woman in a black dress and a white apron, with forearms that have stirred a great deal and a wooden spoon she points with.
A gold crucifix on a chain, and a burn on the inside of her wrist the shape of a ladle’s rim.
Black hair in a net, going white at the front in a streak she calls her medal.

ask: My night. I was on my feet. Write that down first.
Ask. I answer. Then I go home and sit down, and God help the man who asks me anything after that.
deflect: You want to know that, you ask the saints. They see everything and they don’t cook.
Not my business. My business is the stove.
nobodyElse: Nobody. Me. That’s enough.
Nobody else. I don’t need company. I have the stove.

hours.7: Seven, my feet start to hurt. They hurt till Sunday.
hours.8: Eight, I want my supper. A cook never eats her own supper. Ask any cook.
hours.9: Nine, my Rosa and the babies come into my head, and I get cross with whoever is closest.
hours.10: Ten, the day should be over, and the day doesn’t listen.
hours.11: Eleven, I pray a little. Mostly for my feet.

refuse: No. You want that, you go to confession and ask the priest what I told him.
I said no. I say no to the head waiter forty times a night. I can say it to you.
ownUp: Va bene. I tell you, and then I go home.

ties.line: Abe Sokol asked me to marry him once, over a tray of rolls. The rolls were better than the question.
Demos talks to the customers like they’re dukes and to me like I’m the stove.
Yetta Sobel brought all five of mine into the world. Thursdays I feed her, and she cheats at pinochle like a saint.
Carmine married my Rosa and gave her a fur coat and a card room. I’d have settled for the coat.

secrets.text: She carries the last of the soup home in a covered pot for her daughter’s family and crosses it off the slate herself, which is why there is never any soup.

asVictim.why: She knows what goes into everything at Steinmetz’s, and what goes out the alley door.
asVictim.foundWith: a covered pot of soup, still warm, and her wooden spoon in her apron pocket.

doing: writing in a rent book with a fountain pen
counting bills with a rubber thumb
looking at a banister as if it owed her money
drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in

looks.text: A stout woman in gray, buttoned to the throat, carrying a leather satchel with a brass lock on it.
A pince-nez on a black ribbon, which she puts on to read a rent book and takes off to read a face.
A stout woman in the hall reading the names on the mailboxes as if they were a list of debts, which to her they are.

ask: My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order.
I’ll answer you the way I answer everything: in writing, if you like, and in ink.
deflect: That isn’t in the book.
I collect rents. I don’t collect gossip; it doesn’t pay on the first.
nobodyElse: No one else. I prefer it that way. People in company tend to want extensions.
Nobody. Write it down: nobody.

hours.7: Seven, a boiled egg and a slice of toast. Thirty years. It’s cheaper than variety.
hours.8: Eight, I do the arithmetic. It is never in my favor and never wrong.
hours.9: Nine is a good hour for rent: people are fed, and home, and feeling guilty.
hours.10: Ten, I think about the first of the month. I always think about the first of the month.
hours.11: Eleven, I wind my watch. Mr. Krantz used to wind it for me. Now I do it, and it keeps better time.

refuse: That account is closed.
No. You may put that in your book, and I will put it in mine.
ownUp: Let us balance the books, then.

ties.line: Wojcik is a good janitor when he’s awake, which is mostly when I’m in the building.
Francis Doyle courted me for a year in nineteen-four and then married the alderman’s niece. He’s been an alderman’s clerk ever since. I call that justice.
Miss Marsh is two months behind and tells me the money’s tied up in stock. Her stock is a tray of cigarettes.
Mr. Belkin borrowed a hundred dollars from me in a voice that made it sound like a favor to me.

secrets.text: She keeps two rent books for the Orchard Street building, one for her late husband’s estate and one for herself, and the third floor pays into the second.

asVictim.why: Half the tenants on Orchard Street owe her, and the other half are about to.
asVictim.foundWith: her satchel locked and still in her hand, and the key on a ribbon round her neck.

doing: shaking hands with a man who didn’t offer his
handing out cigars with the alderman’s name on the band
writing a name in a little black book
eating a free lunch somebody else is paying for

looks.text: A florid man in a derby and a checked waistcoat, with a carnation in his buttonhole that the alderman pays for.
A right hand already out and reaching for yours from across the room.
A little black notebook in his waistcoat pocket, held shut with a rubber band, which he pats when he says he’ll see what he can do.

ask: My friend! Of course. Between you and me and the alderman, I’ve nothing to hide, and I’ll prove it at length.
Where was I? Serving the public, my friend, as always. Let me tell you how.
deflect: Now that’s a question for the alderman, and the alderman’s a busy man.
I’ll see what I can do. Which is to say, no.
nobodyElse: Nobody else, on my honor, and my honor’s registered with the county.
Alone, my friend. A rare thing for me. Nobody to shake hands with.

hours.7: Seven, I’m a public servant still. The public doesn’t stop needing things at six.
hours.8: Eight’s a good hour for a favor. People have eaten. They’re grateful.
hours.9: Nine, it’s November on my mind. A man in my line always has November on his mind.
hours.10: Ten, I start remembering who I promised what. It’s a long list. I keep it short by forgetting.
hours.11: Eleven, I’m tired of being liked. It’s harder work than people think.

refuse: I can’t comment on that, my friend. I’m not authorized, and I’m not inclined.
No comment. Write that down; it’s the most honest thing I’ve said all week.
ownUp: Off the record, then. Everything’s off the record with me, ask anyone.

ties.line: Ruby Szabo blames me for her brother. Her brother blames the dice. I’m with the brother.
Bertha would have made a fine wife for a man with nerves of iron. I went into politics instead; it’s quieter.
Teitel owes me ten dollars for his pushcart license, and a little gratitude, and I’d settle for the ten.
Amato drives like he votes: wherever he likes. I had his license looked at. Civic duty.

secrets.text: He collects an envelope from the Peacock every Friday for the alderman, and the alderman gets half of what’s in it.
He rents the empty flat on the sixth floor of the Excelsior as a Mr. Smith, for meetings the alderman doesn’t know about.

asVictim.why: He has kept a little black book of favors for twenty years, and every name in it would like the book back.
asVictim.foundWith: a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it.

doing: correcting an exercise book in red pencil
winding a metronome
playing a nocturne very slowly with the soft pedal down
drinking tea from a cup with a saucer, always the saucer

looks.text: A thin, straight-backed woman in a gray dress with a white collar, sitting at an upright piano with the lid shut.
Hair in a tight bun with a pencil through it, which she uses, and a second pencil, which she forgets.
Long fingers that tap out scales on whatever’s in front of them: a table, a banister, your sleeve.

ask: Certainly. I shall be brief and in tempo.
My evening was quiet, and I could be quiet about it, but since you ask, here it is.
deflect: That is not a question I was brought up to answer.
I teach the piano. I don’t teach that.
nobodyElse: No one else. I prefer an empty room. It doesn’t play wrong notes.
Alone, and glad of it.

hours.7: Seven is the hour every child on Orchard Street practices badly at once. You can hear it from anywhere.
hours.8: Eight, I make tea. A proper cup, with a saucer, whatever else is happening.
hours.9: Nine is for music I play for myself. Slow music. Nobody needs to hear it.
hours.10: Ten I go to bed, generally. ‘Generally’ is a word I use a great deal.
hours.11: Eleven is far too late for anything decent, and I say so to anybody who’s up.

refuse: I don’t care to discuss it, and I won’t be made to.
No. I can be very firm with a child of eight. I can be firmer with you.
ownUp: Since we are being honest, and apparently we are, I shall play it as written.

ties.line: Miriam fixed my front tooth for nothing in nineteen-sixteen. I have been paying her back in Sunday lunches ever since, and we are nowhere near square.
Mr. Mabry tells my pupils that scales are for fish. Three of them have taken up the cornet.
Agnes Nowak owes me for nine lessons and has learned, as far as I can tell, one.

secrets.text: She plays piano at the Peacock two nights a week in a red wig, as Bunny LaRue, and her pupils’ mothers would die.

asVictim.why: She has a sharp tongue, and one of the people it has been sharp with knows about the red wig in her music case.
asVictim.foundWith: her music case, with a red wig folded inside it on top of the Czerny.

doing: sleeping in his cab with his cap over his face
eating a sandwich on the running board
polishing the radiator cap with his sleeve
arguing with a horse cab about the right of way

looks.text: A stocky man in a leather jacket and a chauffeur’s cap pushed back, moving a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other to show he’s thinking.
Hands black to the wrist from the engine, and a clean handkerchief in his top pocket for the passengers.
A St. Christopher medal on a chain round his neck and another on the dashboard of his cab, in case one of them is off duty.

ask: Where to? Ha. Sorry. Habit. Go ahead, ask.
My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter.
deflect: I just drive. People get in, people get out. I don’t look in the mirror.
Couldn’t say. My eyes were on the road, and the road was empty.
nobodyElse: Nobody in the back. Flag up.
Just me. Not a fare all night, and you can tell my mother.

hours.7: Seven’s the worst hour for a cab. Everybody’s late, and everybody thinks it’s my fault. I take seven off when I can.
hours.8: Eight, I eat. Most men eat sitting at a table. I’m not most men.
hours.9: Nine’s dead. Nine’s always dead. You could roll a bowling ball down Delancey at nine.
hours.10: Ten, the shows let out and everybody wants Brooklyn. Nobody wants Brooklyn at any other hour.
hours.11: Eleven, I think about quitting. Every night at eleven I think about it, and every morning I’ve forgotten.

refuse: No. That fare I’m not taking.
Meter’s off. I’m not saying.
ownUp: Flag down. Here’s the real route.

ties.line: Oscar knows everybody’s business by their watch. Good kid. Talks too much in the back seat.
Tillie and me went steady all last summer. Then she got a part. I still don’t take her fare. I can’t help it.
Doyle had my hack license pulled for a week because I wouldn’t drive his cousin for nothing. A week is a lot of fares.

secrets.text: Some nights he runs crates up from the river for Sokol with his flag down, and unloads them through the bakery door.

asVictim.why: He has driven everybody on the East Side somewhere they’d rather nobody knew about.
asVictim.foundWith: his cap and a trip sheet in his pocket with every fare written down in pencil.

doing: telling somebody what they weighed at birth
knitting a baby’s cap of no particular size
drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth
complaining to the janitor through the radiator

looks.text: A tiny old woman in a black shawl, carrying a doctor’s bag older than most of the people she brought into the world.
Spectacles on a chain, and a face that has seen everybody on Orchard Street at their very first and is not impressed by their since.
A small woman in a second-floor kitchen doorway, in a hairnet and felt slippers, holding a glass of tea in a saucer.

ask: Sit, sit. I delivered half this street. I can deliver an evening.
You want to know where I was? Pull up a chair. It’s not a short story; I’m an old woman.
deflect: I’ve delivered nine hundred babies. Not one of them asked me that.
That, I don’t know, and at my age, what I don’t know, I don’t need.
nobodyElse: Nobody. Me and my feet.
Nobody else, and I’d know. I know everybody. I was there when they arrived.

hours.7: Seven, I eat a little something. A midwife eats when she can, because the babies don’t ask.
hours.8: Eight, my feet go up, wherever I am. They’ve earned it.
hours.9: Nine, I knit. Caps for babies not born yet. I have a feeling about who’s next.
hours.10: Ten, I think about my late husband, may he rest. He’s resting. He was always good at it.
hours.11: Eleven, I should be asleep, and I tell the whole street to be asleep, and the whole street hasn’t listened to me since the day it was born.

refuse: No. I’ve kept more secrets than the priest and the rabbi together, and I won’t start telling at my age.
That one stays in the bag.
ownUp: Well. It comes out eventually. They always do.

ties.line: Wojcik heats the building like it’s his money. It’s not his money. It’s barely his building.
Assunta feeds me Thursdays. I delivered her five, so she figures she’s still paying.
Solomon sells neckties off a cart and thinks he’s a merchant prince. My daughter married his son, so I nod.

secrets.text: She reads coffee grounds for a quarter at a back table in Sokol’s, and her rabbi thinks she’s at her sister’s.

asVictim.why: She knows the real birthday of everybody on Orchard Street, and the real father of a few.
asVictim.foundWith: her doctor’s bag, and in it a half-knitted baby’s cap and a list of names in Yiddish.

doing: painting her nails a red her landlady disapproves of
saying ‘Number, please’ in her sleep
counting out change for a horse she likes
writing a letter home to Scranton

looks.text: Pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide.
Nails painted red and bitten, both.
A girl in a kimono halfway up the second flight with her shoes in her hand, stopped as if somebody had called her name.

ask: Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through.
I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job.
deflect: I’m sorry, that line’s busy.
I’m not supposed to listen in, so I don’t know anything.
nobodyElse: Nobody, and I’m disconnecting.
That’s all. Nobody on the line.

hours.7: Seven, I still hear the switchboard in my ears. It takes till eight to stop.
hours.8: Eight’s when I feel lucky. I don’t know why. It’s cost me a fortune.
hours.9: Nine’s for Scranton. You’d be amazed how much I think about Scranton for somebody who left it.
hours.10: Ten I’m supposed to be in. Rule four. I know rule four by heart.
hours.11: Eleven, I wish I was asleep and I wish I was dancing, both at once.

refuse: I’m sorry, I can’t connect you.
No. Please. I can’t.
ownUp: I’ll tell you. Only please don’t tell Mrs. Rafferty; she’s got a page for me already.

ties.line: Mrs. Rafferty’s writing it down. I’ve seen the book. My name’s got its own page.
I owe Mr. Fishel eleven dollars on a horse called Mother’s Pride. Mother’s Pride is a liar.
I owe Miss Lowenthal for nine lessons. She says I play like I haven’t paid. I haven’t.

secrets.text: She goes dancing at the Peacock on the nights she tells Mrs. Rafferty she’s working the late shift at the exchange.

asVictim.why: She listens in at the switchboard, and somebody found out what she heard.
asVictim.foundWith: her shoes in her hand and a dance card from the Peacock in her coat pocket.

doing: arranging neckties on his cart by color, then by price, then by color again
haggling with a customer who has already paid
eating a baked potato from a street stove
tying a tarpaulin over his cart for the night

looks.text: An old man in two overcoats, the outer one open and the inner one buttoned, with a dozen neckties hung over one arm for display.
A necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others.
A white beard trimmed square, and fingerless gloves from which he can produce change faster than you can see it.

ask: For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen.
Sit, sit. My night you can have, and a tie to go with it.
deflect: That, I don’t sell.
What do I know? I sell neckties. A necktie doesn’t ask where a man’s been.
nobodyElse: Nobody. Not a customer. Not a policeman.
Nobody else. I’d have tried to sell them something.

hours.7: Seven, I count the day. It never takes long.
hours.8: Eight, my wife starts saying, Solomon, you’ll catch your death. Forty years she says it. Forty years I’m alive.
hours.9: Nine, business. I think about it; it doesn’t think about me.
hours.10: Ten, a man my age should be in bed. I tell everybody. Nobody listens to a necktie man.
hours.11: Eleven, I remember my mother, may she rest, who never once told me to sell neckties.

refuse: No sale. Not at any price.
That, I keep under the cloth.
ownUp: Nu, all right. For you, the truth, wholesale.

ties.line: Doyle got me my pushcart license for ten dollars and a vote. He’s had the vote. He’s still waiting for the ten.
Yetta Sobel is my son’s mother-in-law, which means she’s been right about everything since nineteen-twenty.
Mr. Mabry buys a tie off my cart every Saturday and wears it once. He says a bandleader can’t be seen twice in a tie. God bless the bandleader.

secrets.text: He sits in on the late game at the card room over the garage, with the rent money, on nights he tells his wife he’s minding the cart.

asVictim.why: He has held the best corner on Orchard Street for thirty years against all comers, and some of the comers are still waiting.
asVictim.foundWith: a dozen neckties over one arm and his pushcart license, folded small, in his inside pocket.
